title: Retirement plan in school
summary: Corebridge Financial and Miami-Dade County Public Schools are celebrating the 60th anniversary of implementing a 403(b) retirement plan in a public school.
body_text: This month, Corebridge Financial and Miami-Dade County Public Schools are commemorating one of the earliest implementations of a 403(b) retirement plan in a public school. In October 1964, The Variable Annuity Life Insurance Company (VALIC), a Corebridge Financial company, issued a 403(b) plan to a teacher at Coral Gables Elementary who enrolled at $25 per pay period, helping to pioneer 403(b) employer contracts for educators in the United States. To help us celebrate this milestone, Frank Buggs, a retired educator from Miami-Dade County Public Schools and one of our longest 403(b) workplace retirement plan participants, shared his thoughts about retirement and his long-lasting relationship with Corebridge. Frank, who opened his Corebridge account fifty-five years ago, has been enjoying retirement for the last twenty-six years as a father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. Q. At Corebridge, we believe "action is everything" when it comes to making goals and dreams become reality. What does "action is everything" mean to you? A. Without action, I wouldn’t have anything. With action, I’m having a good retirement. Q. How has Corebridge helped you prepare for retirement? A. I’ve been very happy with Corebridge, especially the service I received from their financial professionals. They’ve helped me keep up with my financial situation and met with me annually to review my plan. Q. How has your Corebridge financial professional helped you in your retirement confidence? A. When I first started teaching, I lived paycheck to paycheck. The best advice I received from a Corebridge financial professional was to start investing, and they provided guidance and advice. Q. What advice would you give a new teacher about saving for retirement? A. Start investing in your 403(b) retirement plan now, so you will have a better financial future. This interview is published for educational use only, and is not intended to provide financial, legal, fiduciary, accounting, or tax advice, nor is it intended to make any investment or insurance recommendations. Experiences presented may not be representative of the experiences of other individuals and there is no guarantee of similar results or success. Responses have been edited for clarity. Please consult with the appropriate legal, financial, or tax professional regarding your own financial situation and investment needs and objectives.

title: Are You a "Da Gong Ren"? 5 Viral Workplace Slang Words Chinese Gen Z is Obsessed With
summary: Master Chinese reading from HSK 1–6 through real stories and culture. Read Bean personalizes each lesson with smart review and context to help you improve effortlessly.
body_text: If you’ve been scrolling through TikTok or Instagram Reels lately, you’ve probably noticed a fascinating shift in internet culture. Young creators are obsessing over the hilarious, brutally honest, and deeply relatable world of Chinese workplace slang. Gone are the days when textbooks only taught you stiff phrases like "Manager, this is my report." Today’s generation uses sharp humor to bond over corporate life. Whether you are navigating a job in a Chinese-speaking environment or just want to understand the viral memes on your feed, here are 5 trending workplace slang words you need to know to sound like a true native. 1. 打工人 (Dǎ Gōng Rén) – The "Wage Slave" Pride This is the ultimate anthem of the modern working class. While it technically translates to "working person," 打工人 carries a badge of sarcastic honor. It describes anyone clocking in to make a living, from office interns to corporate executives. The Vibe: It’s used to build camaraderie. On social media, you’ll see people posting morning coffee selfies with the caption: "Good morning, Da Gong Ren! Let’s secure that bread!" 2. 班味 (Bān Wèi) – The "Smell of Work" Ever looked in the mirror after an exhausting 9-to-5 and realized your sparkle is completely gone? That is exactly what 班味 means. It refers to the unpolished, tired, and deeply drained aura that corporate life leaves on a person. The Vibe: Creators love posting "Before vs. After" transformations on Instagram—showing how they look vibrant on the weekend versus how they look completely covered in ban wei by Tuesday afternoon. 3. 内卷 (Nèi Juǎn) – "Involution" / Endless Rat Race Originally an academic term, 内卷 has become a massive internet buzzword. It describes a situation where everyone is working harder and harder, but the rewards stay exactly the same because the competition is too fierce. The Vibe: Think of an office where one person stays until 8 PM, so the next person stays until 9 PM, and soon everyone is sleeping at their desks just to keep up. That is peak nei juan . 4. 摸鱼 (Mō Yú) – "Slacking Off" (Literally: Catching Fish) Derived from the old Chinese idiom "catching fish in muddy waters," 摸鱼 is the ultimate counter-attack to corporate exhaustion. It means to secretly slack off or do personal tasks during paid working hours. The Vibe: Filling up your water bottle 15 times a day, taking a 30-minute bathroom break, or hiding a miniature game tab behind your excel sheet? Congratulations, you are an expert at mo yu . 5. 躺平 (Tǎng Píng) – "Lying Flat" When the nei juan (rat race) gets to be too much, Gen Z chooses to 躺平 . This means refusing to overwork, resetting your expectations, and doing the bare minimum to survive comfortably rather than stressing over a promotion. The Vibe: It’s the ultimate form of peaceful silent quitting. It’s all about choosing mental health and work-life balance over burning out for a corporate ladder. title: Choosing the right AI solution: Five build or buy mistakes to avoid (and what to do instead)
summary: Five common mistakes organizations make when deciding on their AI investment, along with examples and recommendations on more effective approaches.
body_text: Explore key topics in this blog Mistake #1: Believing AI can solve every problem Mistake #2: Focusing on GenAI and not exploring all available AI and non-AI options Mistake #3: Not anchoring decisions in your organization’s strategies and capabilities Mistake #4: Custom-building a solution without considering existing options Mistake #5: Chasing the latest tools without clear objectives Contact CGI to find answers to these and other AI questions As a data scientist and AI expert, I work with clients on both AI strategy and hands-on solution design. One of the biggest challenges they face is navigating the “build or buy” question: Should we build an AI solution or buy one off the shelf? This sounds like a straightforward question, but the reality is more complex. The market is becoming crowded with AI solutions, and board members, stakeholders, internal teams and consumers often have conflicting demands on how to adopt AI and its proper use. This creates pressure to not only make quick decisions, but the right ones. To help you navigate these complexities, here are five common mistakes organizations make when deciding on their AI investment, along with examples and recommendations on more effective approaches. Mistake #1: Believing AI can solve every problem When I first meet with clients, they are often surprised when I begin by asking: “Does your organization really need AI?” Surprisingly, the answer is sometimes no. Many clients assume AI can solve everything, but this can lead to overcomplicated and costly solutions when simpler approaches could work better. Client example: Government agency with mismatched datasets Challenge : A government agency wanted AI to compare two datasets from different systems to understand why they didn’t match. Solution : In this instance, AI wasn’t needed at all. Instead, their need could be addressed by running two daily SQL queries. Recommendation : Start with your problem, not the technology. Depending on your goals, non-generative AI, or even non-AI solutions, can be cheaper and better suited for your needs. Read more on this topic from my colleague Diane Gutiw: Let’s stop talking about AI . Mistake #2: Focusing on GenAI and not exploring all available AI and non-AI options Despite being around for decades, many still equate AI with GenAI (e.g., LLMs and chatbots). While GenAI solutions are undeniably useful, there are other AI and non-AI tools that can be more accurate and cost effective. Client example: Extracting information from documents Challenge : A client wanted to use a large vision model to extract information from multiple reports. Solution : A traditional OCR (Optical Character Recognition) tool like Tesseract, built specifically for this purpose, provided the client with greater precision and efficiency—without the use of GenAI. Recommendation : Explore the full range of existing technologies and solutions. Compare GenAI with traditional approaches, and consider combining tools (e.g., OCR with GenAI) to yield better results. Read more on this topic from my colleague Dave Henderson: AI is more than just GenAI . Mistake #3: Not anchoring decisions in your organization’s strategies and capabilities Your organization's digital strategies and capabilities should form the foundation of your build or buy decision. Keep in mind: AI is not one-size-fits all. The same solution can produce different outcomes between organizations, depending on their business processes. Client example: Choosing a solution to align with current needs and future strategies Challenge : A client identified a need requiring an external solution but was unsure whether to buy an existing tool or custom-build one. Solution : While not the only factor, a good starting point when making your decision is reviewing your organization’s IT footprint and strategy. From there, options include: Engaging partners to build AI solutions that they later manage in-house. Partnering with vendors like CGI to not only build solutions but also maintain and continually update. Using an off-the-shelf product can be faster and more affordable. Recommendation : Align your AI investment with your digital strategy and capabilities. Engage vendors to evaluate solutions based on your organization’s needs, not what worked for others. Mistake #4: Custom-building a solution without considering existing options Clients sometimes assume they need specific customizations, but often there are off-the-shelf solutions with embedded AI or have features that could meet their needs in the future. Client example: Build or buy a data query solution? Challenge : CGI builds custom Ask Data AI solutions that can work across multiple sources like Databricks and Snowflake. There are also off-the-shelf tools and platforms embedded with AI capabilities. In cases like this, should they build or buy? Solution : For smaller organizations that store data within one source, there isn’t always a need to build a custom solution because the AI capabilities within off-the-shelf solutions are sufficient. However, when needs become more complex—such as multiple data platforms or deep domain knowledge requirements—customization can be the better path. Recommendation : Work with service providers or a trusted third-party to see if your needs can be met with existing or tailored solutions. CGI has alliances and advanced insight into product roadmaps across providers and solutions to help you make informed decisions. Read more about the client story above: GenAI cuts query response time to just 45 seconds for telecom firm . Mistake #5: Chasing the latest tools without clear objectives The pace of AI advancements and new tools can be overwhelming to track and integrate into your workflows and solutions. Client example: Existing AI solution overtaken by new tools Challenge : A client needed to choose between an existing AI solution and new tools with extra capabilities. Solution : Despite the features newer options offered, the original solution still generated accurate results, strong ROI and time-savings—making a replacement unnecessary. Recommendation : Focus decisions on your business objectives. Continually assess new tools with the help of AI experts or trusted partners, but weigh them against your objectives and performance goals. With AI, it’s not just about its capabilities. Factors like security, trust, data and regulatory can introduce complexity not previously found in non-AI solutions.
